open-question.question: In the rewritten enumeration step of alternatives-procedure.md, is the enumerator told to first identify the axes of the decision and derive the options from them, or are distinctness and coverage stated only as properties the finished set must have?
open-question.alternative: Step 2 of alternatives-procedure.md opens with a required move: name the axes the underlying decision turns on, then build the options as positions on those axes (on a multi-axis question, as combinations weighed in reasoning), and state distinctness and coverage as the tests the resulting set must pass. Axis identification comes before any candidate is drafted, and the step is mandatory. The goal already has each option state where it stands on each axis and has every combination weighed on a multi-axis question, and both assume the axes were named first. A generation step targets the recorded failure mode directly: 12 overrides took a combination on an axis the set never laid out, and 20 took a direction no option represented. The fixed step is also something the one-off re-run can check. It is the most prescriptive wording. It adds a step to every enumeration, including the inline one in discuss-open-question, and on a plainly one-axis question it can produce invented axes or a mechanical cross-product that pads the set. The axes are never rendered, because the tool gives a block no place for a statement about the whole set, so the step shows only indirectly, through each option's what-it-is prose.

The enumerator drafts candidates freely as now, and then must name the axes the decision turns on and check the draft against them: add a missing position or viable combination, and merge any two options that do not differ in substance on some axis. Axis identification comes after drafting, as a required check. Candidates are still generated naturally from the question, and a concrete audit is added that catches near-duplicates (13 historical sets held them) as well as gaps. The audit can be written as a short check at the end of the step instead of a rewrite of how options are produced. The draft anchors on the question's wording, which is where the misses come from, so axes read off the drafted candidates tend to be the axes those candidates already vary on. An axis none of them varies on can stay invisible to the audit, and not doing the thing at all is the most frequent missing direction.

Step 2 says only what the finished set must be: every two options differ in substance on at least one axis, and the set covers the underlying decision rather than the question's wording. It prescribes no method for reaching that. Axis identification is never required. It is the shortest and least prescriptive rewrite. It keeps the procedure describing outcomes, as the current "complete now" sentence does, leaves the enumerator free to reason however suits the question, and avoids ritual steps on simple questions. The current rule already requires a complete set without saying how to reach one, and the benchmark shows that property-level wording let directions and combinations go missing. It also asks each option to state its position on axes the enumerator was never told to identify, so the requirement can be met in name while the axes stay implicit.

Distinctness and coverage are the binding requirements. Naming the decision's axes and deriving options from them is offered as the recommended way to meet them, not as a mandatory step, so the enumerator can skip it where the axes are obvious. Axis identification comes first but is optional. It points the enumerator at the method that produces covering sets without forcing it on one-axis questions, so it avoids most of the padding risk of a mandatory step while still putting axes in front of the model. An optional method is the easiest part of the wording to skip, and the runs most likely to skip it are the hurried ones that miss directions. The softer wording also makes the one-off check harder to read, because a shortfall could come from the rule or from the step being skipped.

open-question.question: Does the enumeration step of alternatives-procedure.md carry its own explicit instruction to weigh the direction of not doing the thing the question is about, or is that direction left to follow from the general coverage requirement?
open-question.alternative: Step 2 of alternatives-procedure.md gets its own instruction, separate from the general coverage requirement, telling the enumerator to weigh the direction of not doing the thing the question is about on every question. The enumerator lists that direction as an option when it is honestly viable and leaves it out otherwise, with no dedicated place to record that it was considered. It targets the gap the benchmark aggregate names as the most frequent missing direction. The goal calls out this direction by name. The procedure's current requirement that the set be "complete now" already implied coverage and still missed it in practice, so a separate instruction is the most likely to change what the enumerator produces. It singles out one direction among the many the coverage rule is supposed to reach. Because it applies to every question, it pulls against the procedure's existing ban on strawmen and padding: the enumerator may add a token "don't do it" option where no one would really choose it. The block also has nowhere to record that the direction was weighed and rejected.

Step 2 states the general coverage requirement (the set covers the underlying decision, not the question's wording) and names not doing the thing, where honestly viable, as an example within that same sentence, following the goal's own parenthetical. There is no separate instruction and no check the enumerator must run on every question. It makes the most frequently missed direction visible where the enumerator reads the coverage rule, without adding a special-case rule or a per-question step. The procedure stays one general principle, and the wording tracks the goal closely. An example inside a general rule is weaker than an instruction and can be skimmed past. If the rewritten wording is not enough, the milestone's one-off re-run may still show sets that miss the direction, which weakens the case that the change is verified.

Step 2 states only the general coverage requirement, that the set covers the underlying decision rather than the question's wording. Dropping the thing is never mentioned and is expected to follow from applying that requirement. It keeps the enumeration rules to general principles with no special cases, so the procedure does not privilege one direction and adds no pressure to pad sets with a "don't do it" option where it isn't viable. The existing requirement that the set be "complete now" was already general and still let this direction go missing more often than any other, so relying on generality alone may not change behaviour. Whether this option is enough depends on how strongly the separately open rules on premise rejection and axis identification are written.

open-question.question: Does the enumeration step of alternatives-procedure.md tell the enumerator to find what the question's wording takes for granted and weigh rejecting it, or is covering the underlying decision stated without such a step?
open-question.alternative: The enumeration step of alternatives-procedure.md gets its own instruction: before listing options, name what the question's wording takes for granted (an assumed need, mechanism, or framing), then for each such premise weigh an option that rejects it, and list that option only where it is honestly viable. On the axes it touches, this option adds a dedicated process step, so a premise is examined on every question and not only when the enumerator happens to notice it. It targets a failure the benchmark aggregate shows directly: 9 of 106 overriding answers rejected a premise that every listed option shared. A named step makes the enumerator look for exactly the assumption that a wording-bound set carries silently, rather than hoping the general coverage requirement brings it up. It lengthens a procedure that every alternatives subagent and discuss-open-question follow on every question, although most questions have no premise worth rejecting. It also invites premise-rejecting options that are really strawmen, which works against the existing ban on padding. How much it overlaps other rules depends on how the Drop-it direction rule and Axis identification step siblings settle, because not doing the thing is itself the rejection of one premise.

The enumeration step says only that the set must cover the underlying decision and not the question's wording, with no step for finding premises. Spotting and rejecting a premise is left to the enumerator's judgment under that one requirement, and premise problems on the authoring side are left to the "shared premises" idea document the milestone writes under temp/. It keeps the procedure short and states the outcome without prescribing a method, the same approach step 2 already takes with "complete now". It adds no rule that could push premise-rejecting options into a set whose premises are sound. The current procedure already asks for completeness without defining it, and the historical sets still missed shared premises. A bare "underlying decision" requirement may be too abstract to change what the enumerator actually does, and nothing points it at the particular assumption every option shares.

There is no process step. Instead, the coverage requirement comes with one concrete test the finished set must pass: if every listed option shares an assumption the question's wording introduced, the set must either include an option that rejects that assumption or leave it out only because rejecting it is not viable in this project. The check sits in step 2 next to the completeness requirement. It aims precisely at the benchmark category, a premise that every option shared, while leaving the enumeration method free. Because the test only fires when all the options agree on an assumption, it adds nothing to sets that already vary on it. Running the test still requires the enumerator to see the shared assumption, which is the step that failed in the historical cases, so it may catch little more than the bare property does. A self-check the finished set must pass is also harder to verify in the one-off re-run than a visible step.

Premise-finding is folded into the enumeration's axis work rather than stated as a rule of its own: each assumption the wording takes for granted is treated as one more axis of the decision, with accepting and rejecting it as its values, so rejecting a premise comes out of the same step that lays out the other axes. A single mechanism covers both the axes the question names and the ones its wording hides, so the procedure gains no separate premise rule. A premise-rejecting option then carries its stance on every other axis like any other option, and does not stand outside the set's structure. It only works if the enumeration step contains an explicit axis step, so its viability depends on how the Axis identification step sibling settles. Treating every premise as an axis also multiplies the combinations the goal says must all be weighed, and on a multi-axis question that can make the set grow more than the problem requires.

open-question.question: When several candidate options are one approach at different degrees or parameter values, how does the alternative set represent that approach?
open-question.alternative: The approach appears once in the set as a single alternative. Its what-it-is text names the approach and the range its degree or parameter can take, and leaves the value unset so that whoever answers supplies it. The set stays small and every pair of options still differs in approach, which is the distinctness the goal asks for. It also matches how answers already arrive: of the 106 overrides, 65 refined a listed option rather than leaving the set, and that is the path that supplies the value. Some answer paths record the lifted what-it-is text as the decision word for word. `Alternative-answer:` does this, and a recommendation's rationale does it too unless it names a value. On those paths, accepting the option records an approach with no value, so `## Decisions` holds an incomplete decision that task derivation or completion must fill in without a recorded basis.

The degree counts as an axis like any other. The set lists a separate alternative for each degree or value at which the key advantage or drawback genuinely changes. Values whose trade-off is the same are merged into one option, described by its range. Every alternative that is lifted or recommended records a concrete, usable decision. The trade-off between degrees is visible to the pick instead of being hidden inside one option. Deciding whether a trade-off "genuinely changes" is the same judgment that let near-duplicates through before (13 of the historical sets held them). The set also grows by one option per threshold, and on a multi-axis question that growth multiplies across combinations.

The approach appears once, fixed at one stated value the enumerator considers most defensible. The other values are mentioned only in its drawback, as ways it could be tuned. The set stays compact and each option still lifts as a complete decision, with no value missing on any answer path. Choosing the value is a preference, and `alternatives-procedure.md` states that the enumeration half forms none. The other values are also never options, so the recommendation pass can never pick one: a better value can only arrive as a manual override. That is the kind of gap the milestone sets out to close.

alternative.id: Single option, value as follow-up question

open-question.alternative: The approach appears once with its value left open, and the procedure says the value is a separate decision. After the approach is chosen, `review-milestone-requirements` authors that value as its own one-axis question. This fits the one-axis authoring the goal sets for review. Each recorded decision is complete for the one axis it covers, and the value gets its own properly enumerated set instead of being decided implicitly. It costs an extra review cycle and a further question for every such approach. It depends on the review pass noticing an approach recorded without its value. And the enumeration procedure would have to describe another skill's authoring behaviour, which it currently never does.

The procedure says nothing specific about degree variants. The general rule that every two alternatives differ in substance on at least one axis decides each case. No extra wording goes into the enumeration step, and no answer path, rendering, or tool behaviour changes. A difference in degree can be read as a substantive difference on a parameter axis. The general rule then admits exactly the near-duplicate options it was meant to prevent, and different enumerators may split the same approach in different ways. The historical sets already show that problem: 13 of them held near-duplicate options.

open-question.question: Once an option's what-it-is text must also state where the option stands on each axis, does that field of alternatives-procedure.md keep its one-sentence limit, get a different stated limit, or carry no limit?
open-question.alternative: The what-it-is field in step 2 of alternatives-procedure.md keeps its "one sentence" limit. That one sentence now has to name the option's position on every axis of the decision, and the agent file's rendering step can keep calling the field "the what-it-is sentence" unchanged. What gets recorded stays short. On the Alternative-answer: path, `lift --alternative` prints `<id> — <what-it-is>`, and that line is folded into `## Decisions` and used as the commit body. With one sentence, a recorded decision stays one crisp line. The limit also keeps rationale in the advantage and drawback fields, and it needs no wording change in core/agents/provide-alternatives-to-open-question.md, discuss-open-question, or capture-milestone-principle-updates. On a question with several axes, a sentence that must place the option on every axis turns into a long run-on or gets clipped. Clipping it drops the very position statements the goal requires. How often this happens depends on how the sibling questions on authoring settle. It bites only if multi-axis questions still reach the alternatives pass.

The one-sentence limit is replaced by a limit that grows with the question's shape. The field allows roughly one short sentence or clause per axis the option takes a position on, so a one-axis question still gets one sentence. The length bound follows the growth the goal expects. A multi-axis option gets room to state every position without running on, and a one-axis option stays as terse as it is today. So the rule scales with the axis count, in keeping with the goal's removal of the fixed count guideline. The bound depends on the enumerator's own count of the axes, so a wrong axis count also bends the length. On multi-axis questions, several sentences now go into the lifted `<id> — <what-it-is>` line folded into `## Decisions`. The tool folds all element text to one line, so that becomes one long line. The agent file's "what-it-is sentence" wording also has to change.

The field gets a different fixed limit that does not depend on the axis count, such as "at most two or three sentences" or "a short paragraph". Within that limit it must state the option's position on each axis. It is simple to state and to check, and it gives multi-axis options noticeably more room than one sentence. It also keeps a hard ceiling, so the lifted decision line in `## Decisions` and in capture's reconstruction can never grow past a known size. The number is arbitrary relative to the question's structure. It still squeezes a question with many interdependent axes, and on one-axis questions it invites padding up to the cap. The procedure otherwise bans padding, and the goal drops a count guideline for exactly this kind of reason.

The sentence count is dropped and replaced by a content bound. The what-it-is text holds only what the option is, meaning its position on each axis, and any reason for or against it belongs in the advantage and drawback fields. Its length then follows from how many positions there are to state. It ties the field to what it is for, not to a number, so it fits every question shape without an arbitrary figure. It also keeps the lifted what-it-is line, which becomes the recorded decision, free of rationale. That line stays a clean statement of what was chosen. A qualitative bound is harder for the subagent to apply consistently than a sentence count, and an enumerator can still write long position prose. With no ceiling, a verbose option carries straight into `## Decisions` and commit bodies, because the tool sets no length limit and only folds the text to one line.

The field states no length limit or scope bound at all. It only has to state where the option stands on each axis, and length is left to the procedure's existing ban on padding and to the enumerator's judgment. This is the smallest change to the procedure's wording. Nothing about the field's form can ever conflict with the requirement to state every axis position, and the field is treated consistently with the goal's removal of the count guideline. Nothing stops the what-it-is text from growing into a paragraph that repeats the advantage and drawback. Such text degrades what `lift --alternative` records as the decision and what capture-milestone-principle-updates reads as each option's what-it-is. It also makes the options that discuss-open-question presents harder to compare.

open-question.question: Is postponing the decision, leaving the question unanswered for a later milestone, a direction an alternative set may list, as distinct from the direction of not doing the thing the question is about?
open-question.alternative: The enumeration step names postponement as its own direction, separate from not doing the thing. A set lists it only when grounding shows it is honestly viable, meaning the milestone's goal does not need the question settled now and a later milestone could settle it. It would be recorded as an `## Out of Scope` or later-milestone decision, because derive-tasks will not start while any question is open. It keeps apart two answers that land differently: dropping the thing is a final rejection, while postponing it leaves the thing possible later. Because each is a separate option, the recommendation pass and the answer sweep can pick and record a deferral without anyone having to override the set. Nearly every question could in principle be postponed, so the enumerator needs a viability test to stop a defer option from being added to every set as filler. The option's what-it-is text also has to state a destination (Out of Scope, or a named later milestone), which the enumerator may have no grounds to choose.

Postponement is not a separate direction. It counts as one form of the "not in this milestone" direction, so a set lists at most one option for not doing the thing now, and the answer text says whether that means never or later. Sets stay lean because two options that look almost the same to the pick never appear side by side. That fits the milestone's rule that every two alternatives must differ in substance. It also avoids a second viability judgment. It merges a final rejection with a postponement. The difference then appears only if the user writes a literal answer, and a recommendation or alternative lift records the "not now" option without saying which one was meant.

An alternative set covers only the substantive directions of the underlying decision and never lists postponement. Postponing is treated as something done to the question, not an answer to it: the user can always record it through a literal answer, and review-milestone-requirements can flag a question that lies outside the goal. Every set stays about the decision itself. A fallback that is always available is never repeated in each block, and the enumerator has no universal escape hatch that could crowd out the harder not-doing direction the goal asks sets to cover. The recommendation pass and the answer sweep can never pick a postponement, because they choose only from the set. A question that honestly should wait for a later milestone therefore always needs a manual override, which is the kind of coverage gap this milestone sets out to close.

open-question.question: When an axis of the underlying decision is already the subject of a sibling open question, does an alternative set's coverage extend to that axis, or does the existing rule that an option answering a sibling is left to that sibling bound it?
open-question.alternative: Keep the existing step-1 rule as the limit on coverage. The set covers only the axes of the underlying decision that no sibling question owns, so no option varies on a sibling-owned axis, and each option's what-it-is text states its position only on the axes this question owns. Each axis is decided in exactly one block. This keeps the rule that siblings supply scope and are never assumed settled, which is what lets the alternatives pass annotate blocks in parallel. It also keeps sets small, so one-axis-per-question authoring actually limits growth. Where a sibling-owned axis constrains this one, no set shows which pairings are unviable. The 12 historical overrides that took a combination on an axis the set never laid out could still fall between two questions, because each block's coverage stops at the boundary.

Retire the rule that an option answering a sibling is left to that sibling. Every axis of the underlying decision is laid out and each option states where it stands on it, including axes a sibling question also owns. This is the most literal reading of the goal's "cover the underlying decision" and "every combination weighed" requirements. Each set becomes a complete map of the decision, so an answer taking a cross-question combination can always find it listed. The same axis gets decided in two blocks. Recording one question's answer can fix a stance on a sibling's axis and conflict with that sibling's later answer, which causes more strip-and-re-run cascades. Stating a position on a sibling axis also comes close to presuming how that sibling settles, which step 2 forbids. Sets grow in exactly the way one-axis authoring is meant to prevent.

Siblings still bound the set, so no option varies on a sibling-owned axis. But the enumeration step now explicitly requires each option to name any sibling-owned axis its viability depends on, stated as a condition in its drawback without naming the expected outcome. This turns today's optional "say so in its drawback" into a required statement. It shows interdependence across questions without duplicating any decision. The recommendation pass gets the constraint in the option text, where it can become a depends-on tag. The block format needs no set-level statement, which the tool would refuse anyway. Unviable pairings are described one option at a time rather than laid out as combinations, so a combination spanning two questions is still never an option anyone can pick. It also adds a duty the enumerator must remember for every option, and the drawback field gets longer.

Siblings bound coverage by default. The one exception is a sibling-owned axis that constrains this question's axis so that not every pairing is viable: then the set lays out the viable combinations across both axes, and each option states its position on both. It targets the missed-combination failure without duplicating independent sibling decisions. Fuller coverage applies only where a single-axis set would really mislead. The enumerator has to judge interdependence per question, a conditional rule that is harder to apply the same way every time. Where it applies, it brings back the double-decided axis and the answer-time conflicts. Its merit turns on how the question of authoring interdependent axes settles, since that question decides whether such pairs reach two blocks in the first place.

open-question.question: What test does review-milestone-requirements apply when authoring a question to decide that a gap holds more than one axis and must be authored as several questions?
When two choices in one gap constrain each other so that not every pairing is viable, does review-milestone-requirements author them as two one-axis questions or as one multi-axis question?
open-question.alternative: review-milestone-requirements authors the coupled choices as one question, as a named exception to the one-axis rule. Both choices are asked at once, and the enumeration excludes the pairings that cannot work: it weighs every combination in reasoning and describes only the viable ones, as the milestone goal already requires for a multi-axis question. The pairings that cannot work are visible and removed in the one place that sees both choices together. Every option in the set is a coherent combination, so any answer, whether a pick, a lifted alternative or a manual answer, records one consistent decision in a single fold. The benchmark's cases of an answer taking a combination the set never laid out are addressed directly. The one-axis authoring rule gets an exception, and review must judge when two choices really constrain each other. Where that judgment is loose, compound questions come back through the exception and the set grows by combinations, which is the growth the upstream rule was meant to prevent. How much this matters depends on how the compound-question test is framed.

review-milestone-requirements always authors the two choices as two one-axis questions, raised in the same pass. Each question's alternatives are enumerated independently, since siblings are scope only and never assumed settled. The pairings that cannot work are left to the existing machinery: the recommendation pass's depends-on tags on the pick, and the cascade in remove --option when an answer is recorded. The one-axis rule has no exception, so review needs no judgment about coupling. Nothing new is added to the authoring step, to the enumeration or to the tool. The constraint is handled by reconciliation that already exists and is tested, and each set stays small and focused on one axis. Each set is enumerated without knowing how the other question will settle, so both sets carry options that are only viable in some pairings. A manual answer or lifted alternative can record a pairing that cannot work, and the cascade only strips dependent picks, never the alternatives. As a result, a combination that neither set lays out stays invisible, which is the benchmark's pattern of an answer taking a combination the set never showed.

review-milestone-requirements authors only the choice that constrains the other as a one-axis question now. It holds back the dependent choice, which a later review pass raises as a new gap once the first choice is recorded, through the step-3 check for gaps that recent decisions exposed. The one-axis rule keeps no exception, and the dependent question's alternatives are enumerated after the constraint is recorded in the Decisions section. The grounding step then already rules out the pairings that cannot work, so no set carries an option that is only viable in some pairings, and the existing review loop does the sequencing. Convergence takes an extra round of review, alternatives, recommendation and answer. The upstream choice is enumerated and picked without its consequences for the dependent choice laid out beside it. When the constraint runs both ways, no choice is clearly upstream, and review must still pick an order arbitrarily. The held-back choice can also be overlooked if a later pass does not recognise it as exposed.

open-question.question: How is the one-axis authoring rule of review-milestone-requirements verified, given that the milestone's one-off check re-runs only the alternatives pass?
Which of the historical cases whose alternative set missed the direction the answer took does the one-off check re-run: every case rated a strong candidate, or a smaller fixed subset?
open-question.alternative: Re-run all 20 historical cases already rated strong candidates for a re-run (16 where the answer took a direction no option represented, 4 where it took a combination on an axis the set never laid out), and add no others. It reuses the already-judged, fixed list, so no case is selected after the new wording exists. Twenty cases are also enough for a share-based pass bar to mean something. It costs twenty grounded runs, and each one needs its own historical project state, however the run-location question settles. The list also holds no case where the answer rejected a premise every option shared, so any premise-related wording gets no evidence from it.

Re-run a smaller subset of the 20 strong candidates, fixed before the enumeration wording is rewritten and drawn in proportion to their mix of coverage gaps and uncrossed-axis combinations. It is the cheapest option in runs, historical checkouts, and the user's time spent reviewing the re-run sets, and fixing it in advance still guards against picking cases the new wording happens to fix. A handful of cases makes any share-based bar coarse, with each case swinging the result by a large step. Only a few combination cases can appear, and premise-shift cases are still absent.

Re-run every historical case whose set missed the direction the answer took, whatever its rating: all 41 (20 coverage gaps, 12 uncrossed-axis combinations, 9 shared-premise rejections). It gives the broadest evidence and is the only option that tests all three missed-direction patterns in full, including the shared-premise pattern the strong-candidate list lacks. It costs about twice the runs and grounding work. The lower-rated cases were judged weaker benchmark material, so they add verdicts that are noisier and harder to judge, which weighs more if a person rather than the agent does the judging.

Re-run a fixed subset chosen before the rewrite to span every missed-direction pattern: a few strong coverage-gap cases, a few strong combination cases, and a few shared-premise cases taken from outside the strong list. Each generic failure pattern the new rules target gets at least some evidence, for far less than re-running every missed case. Each pattern gets only a few cases, so a per-pattern result is anecdotal. The shared-premise cases were never rated strong, so their verdicts rest on weaker material than the rest of the sample.

open-question.question: Does the one-off check also re-run control cases, where the historical alternative set already contained the direction the answer took, to see that the new rules neither lose that direction nor pad the set?
open-question.alternative: The one-off check re-runs only the cases whose historical set missed the answer's direction. Loss of a direction and padding are judged by reading the re-run candidate sets and the rewritten wording, and a proper regression side is left to the benchmark-harness idea document under temp/. This is the smallest and cheapest check. Every re-run goes to the failure the milestone exists to fix, and it adds no case selection or matching work beyond what the candidate cases already need. It cannot show that the new rules keep a direction the old rules already found. It also cannot tell growth the rules call for from padding, because every re-run case is one where the historical set was known to be incomplete. So a regression on the most common kind of question, where the set was already right, would go unseen until later milestones.

The check also re-runs a small fixed sample of the refinement overrides. These are the manual answers (65 of the 106 overrides) that refined an option the historical set already listed. For each, it checks that the re-run set still holds that option's direction and has no near-duplicate or filler options. These cases are closest to the candidates: the same answer path, judged by the same verdicts already in the benchmark material. They show directly whether a set that was already covering stays covering. And because refinement means the historical set was complete on direction, extra options there are a clear sign of padding. It adds re-runs and a second matching judgment. A refinement answer often changes the option's details, so judging whether the re-run holds "the same direction" is fuzzier than for a set-chosen answer. The sample also draws only from cases where the user overrode the set, so the far larger mass of accepted picks goes untested.

The check also re-runs a small fixed sample of questions answered by a listed option unchanged. These are Recommendation-answer or Alternative-answer commits. For each, it checks that the re-run set still holds the chosen option's direction and has not grown with padding. These cases stand for how the pass is normally used: the great majority of recorded answers take an embedded option as it is. The direction to match is exactly one historical alternative, so the "still contains it" judgment is as clean as the check can get. No judged verdicts exist yet for these commits, so selecting the sample is new work, done by hand. And an accepted recommendation shows only that the user found the set good enough, not that it was complete, which makes it a weaker baseline for telling growth the rules call for from padding.

The check re-runs control cases from both pools: some refinement overrides and some set-chosen answers. Each is checked for keeping the chosen direction and for not padding the set. This covers both kinds of regression risk, the overridden-but-covered set and the routine accepted set. So a "no loss, no padding" result says something about the pass as a whole, not about one slice of it. It is the costliest control design: the most re-runs, two ways of selecting cases, and two kinds of matching judgment, all for a one-off check. It also increases the privacy-safe aggregate reporting the milestone must commit, and it duplicates much of what the planned benchmark harness would do systematically.

open-question.question: Does the one-off check also run the unchanged enumeration rules on the same cases with the same model, so that a difference in the result can be attributed to the new wording and not to the model?
open-question.alternative: Run only the rewritten enumeration rules over the chosen cases, and judge each new set against the historical set already on record in the benchmark material, with no fresh run of the unchanged rules. Cheapest and simplest form of the check: it needs half the runs, and there is no need to make the pre-change procedure loadable next to the rebuilt `hosts/claude` tree that the maintainer's install points at. The historical sets came from older models, efforts and procedure versions, often grounded in a different project state. A recovered direction could therefore be the model's doing rather than the new wording's, so the check cannot show that the rewrite caused an improvement. At most it can note this as a caveat.

Run the unchanged `alternatives-procedure.md`, taken from the commit before the rewrite, once on every re-run case with the same model and effort setting as the new-rules run. Compare each case's two sets side by side. Separates the wording's effect from the model's for every case, and costs only one extra run per case. It also shows where the old rules already recover the missing direction with today's model, and where the new rules lose something the old ones found. Doubles the cost of the check and needs the pre-change procedure runnable in the same grounded setting. With a single sample per arm, one lucky or unlucky run can still create or hide a difference, so the attribution holds only for a clear margin. How the pairs are counted also depends on how the pass bar is expressed.

Run both the unchanged and the rewritten rules several times per case with the same model and effort setting, and compare how often each arm's sets contain the previously missing direction. Controls for the model's run-to-run variation as well as the model itself. A difference in hit rate between the arms can be credited to the wording with real confidence. Multiplies the run count and the review load well past a one-off check, since every extra set must be judged for a match. It also turns the result into rates, which the pass bar and whoever judges matches would have to accommodate.

Run the new rules first, then run the unchanged rules with the same model and effort setting only on the cases where the new set recovered the missing direction. The goal is to confirm the old rules would not have recovered it too. Puts the attribution test exactly where a claimed improvement needs it, and costs fewer extra runs than a full paired baseline when the new rules recover only part of the cases. It is lopsided: it never shows cases where the old rules would have done better than the new ones. The cases it baselines are chosen by the new rules' own result, so it can confirm gains but never find losses.

open-question.question: Where does the one-off check run the alternatives pass so that each case is grounded in its historical project state while the repositories the cases come from receive no commits or other changes?
Who decides whether a re-run alternative set contains the direction the historical answer took: the agent carrying out the check, or the user reviewing the sets?
open-question.alternative: The agent running the check decides each match by comparing the re-run set against the missing direction already recorded for that case in the benchmark's judged verdicts, and hands the user only the tally and a short aggregate summary. It takes the least of the user's time and fits a headless or scripted run. It also reuses the same kind of judgment that produced the 20 strong-candidate ratings, so the check measures against the same yardstick that selected its cases. The agent that wrote or ran the new rules is grading its own work, and "contains the direction" is a fuzzy semantic call. A lenient reading of near-misses could pass the change without anyone catching it, and no human ever sees the sets the verdict rests on.

A separate judge agent decides each match. It gets its own context with only the historical answer, the recorded missing direction, and the re-run set, and it is not told which rule version produced the set. The user receives only its verdicts. It removes the self-grading bias of the agent carrying out the check while still asking nothing of the user. Hiding which rules produced each set makes the verdicts comparable across runs. Setting up a separate, blinded judging step adds work to a one-off check. The judge is still a model making a fuzzy call with no human anchor. How much the blinding is worth depends on whether the check also produces sets from the unchanged rules to mix in.

The agent puts each case in front of the user: the historical question, the direction the answer took, and the re-run set. It gives no verdict of its own, and the user decides for every case whether the set contains that direction. The person whose answers produced the overrides decides whether each missing direction now appears, which is the most faithful reading of what "the direction the answer took" meant. The verdict carries no model bias. It costs the most user time, because every case's set must be read in full. User judgments are harder to repeat identically on a later re-run, and the user may not recall the context behind older answers from other projects.

The agent records a verdict and a one-line reason for every case, and the user reviews and confirms or overturns each one before the tally counts. The user holds the final say on every case at a fraction of the reading cost, since each verdict comes with the specific option the agent believes matches. Overturned verdicts also show where the agent's judgment of a match is unreliable. A proposed verdict anchors the reviewer, so review tends to become rubber-stamping and the human check is weaker than it looks. The user still has to open every case, so the saving over judging every set directly may be small.

The agent decides each match and marks as uncertain any case where the closest option is only near the historical direction. The user adjudicates only the uncertain cases, plus optionally a small spot-check of the confident ones. Human attention goes where the call is actually hard, so the user's time grows with the number of ambiguous cases rather than the number of re-run cases. Clear hits and clear misses pass without review. It relies on the agent to know which of its own calls are doubtful. A confidently wrong verdict escapes review unless a spot-check happens to catch it, so the tally is only partly human-verified.

open-question.question: What share of the re-run cases must contain the previously missing direction for the one-off check to count the change as verified?
open-question.alternative: Set a fixed share of more than half: the change counts as verified when most of the re-run cases now contain the direction their historical set missed. The bar is stated as a share, so it applies unchanged whichever set of cases the check re-runs. It is a simple bar that can be failed, and the new rules can reasonably reach it. Some historical misses turned on facts nobody had when the question was asked, so no enumeration rule could recover them. A majority bar leaves room for those cases and still requires the rules to fix the typical miss. The cut-off at one half is arbitrary. The cases are a small, hand-picked set, not a random sample, so a single case can move the result across the line, and the verdict says little about how the rules perform on new questions.

Set a fixed share well above half, around three quarters or more: the change counts as verified only when nearly every re-run case now contains the direction its historical set missed. Passing it is strong evidence that the rewritten enumeration step does what the goal claims, which is to cover the underlying decision, including the direction of not doing the thing. A borderline improvement cannot be reported as success. Some misses may not be recoverable by any enumeration rule, so a failure can reflect the chosen cases rather than the wording. That makes a shortfall more likely, and what happens then depends on how the sibling question on shortfall response settles.

Set no absolute share. The change counts as verified when the new rules recover the missing direction in clearly more of the same cases than the unchanged rules recover when run with the same model. A pass can be credited to the new wording and not to the model. Newer models may already recover some directions that the historical run missed, and an absolute share cannot separate that effect from the wording change. It only means something if the check also runs the unchanged rules, which the sibling question on a baseline run decides. It doubles the number of runs. With a small number of cases it still needs a stated margin for "clearly more", so the arbitrary cut-off is moved, not removed.

Apply a share bar separately to each kind of historical miss: a direction no option represented, a combination on an axis the set never laid out, and a premise every option shared. The change counts as verified only when each kind meets its bar. Each new rule is checked on its own. A pass driven only by the frequent "not doing the thing" misses cannot hide that the rules on combinations or premises had no effect. Split across three kinds, each group holds only a few cases, so each share is very noisy. Every case also needs a category label, which is extra judging work on data that must stay outside the repository.

Set no pass share. The check re-runs the cases, records the aggregate share that now contains the missing direction, and the user decides from that result whether the change is verified. It does not claim statistical meaning for a threshold chosen in advance on a small, non-random set of cases. This suits a check that runs once and whose committed trace is limited to aggregate results by the milestone's privacy rule. The check can no longer fail by a stated rule, so "verified" becomes a judgment made after seeing the result. It also gives the sibling question on shortfall response no defined trigger to act on.

open-question.question: If the one-off check falls short of its bar, does the milestone revise the enumeration wording and re-run the check, or record the shortfall and finish?

Which documents outside core/ are updated to match the new enumeration and authoring rules, among docs/skill-reference.md, claim 4 of docs/design-claims.md with its count of two to four alternatives, and CLAUDE.md?
Does CLAUDE.md gain an invariant entry explaining why alternative sets must be distinct and covering and why the count guideline is gone, or does the procedure's own wording carry that alone?
